name: Hardware and Platform Specific
text:
# Hardware and Platform Specific

Also called: GPU (GLSL/HLSL shader), GPU Shader Rendering

## Overview
Hardware and Platform Specific methods execute volume rendering algorithms directly on the GPU using shader languages ([GLSL](#5184-ray-marching-volume-rendering-glsl.md)/HLSL) or compute models ([CUDA](#3671-dual-contouring-2d-cuda.md)/OpenCL), bypassing the CPU for the heavy lifting of ray marching and [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [S1]. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Tiled Parallel Compositing](1192-tiled-parallel-compositing.md) and [Compute Shader Kernel](1202-compute-shader-kernel.md) by its specific reliance on the graphics pipeline's fragment/vertex shaders or specific vendor APIs (CUDA) rather than generic compute abstractions or tile-based memory optimizations [S1].

## Shared principles

## Subtopics

### [GPU-based Ray-casting for Unstructured Grids](1118-gpu-based-ray-casting-for-unstructured-grids.md)
This method provides a [GPU-based ray-casting](#6283-volume-ray-casting.md) algorithm for volume rendering of unstructured grid data that guarantees accurate rendering results for non-convex meshes. It solves the difficulty of mapping irregular unstructured grid data efficiently to GPU hardware by employing the per-pixel intersection list concept from the Bunyk algorithm to ensure correct visibility sorting. Unlike [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) approaches that must overcome cell ordering and per-cell processing bottlenecks, this method represents intersection lists for all faces as an array using a novel construction algorithm for efficient memory access on the GPU. It extends a prior image-tile-based work distribution method to fit modern GPU architectures, increasing ray-coherency in a thread block and improving memory access efficiency.

### [CUDA Volume Ray Casting](2048-cuda-volume-ray-casting.md)
CUDA Volume [Ray Casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) is a direct volume rendering method that parallelizes the ray casting algorithm on the GPU using the CUDA programming model, avoiding intermediate geometric entities to directly generate 2D images from 3D scalar data sets. It distinguishes itself from shader-based GPU approaches by utilizing explicit CUDA kernels for memory management and computation, offering performance improvements over standard OpenGL-based ray casting implementations. It builds on the general principles of [Direct volume ray casting](1117-direct-volume-ray-casting.md).

### [WebGL Volume Rendering](3243-webgl-volume-rendering.md)
[WebGL Volume Rendering](#3243-webgl-volume-rendering.md) performs [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) within a web browser using the WebGL API, typically leveraging the Three.js library for scene management and shader execution. It solves the problem of interactive 3D visualization of scalar volumes (such as microscopy or medical data) in client-side applications without requiring native plugins or server-side rendering. It is distinguished from other GPU-based methods by its specific implementation constraints and optimizations for the web ecosystem, including the use of `SharedArrayBuffer` for high-performance data transfer and specific handling of cross-origin isolation requirements. Unlike CUDA-based approaches, it runs on the client's GPU via JavaScript bindings, trading some raw performance for accessibility and ease of deployment.

### [Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting](3379-triton-accelerated-volume-raycasting.md)
[Triton-accelerated Volume Raycasting](#3379-triton-accelerated-volume-raycasting.md) is a fused GPU rendering technique that uses the Triton compiler to perform volume raycasting, avoiding the materialization of intermediate ray-sample tensors in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to reduce memory footprint and increase speed. It sets itself apart from standard PyTorch-based raycasting by fusing the ray-marching loop into a single kernel, thereby eliminating the memory bandwidth bottlenecks and cache thrashing that cause super-linear performance degradation in non-fused implementations at high resolutions.

### [Efficient Ray Casting Pipeline](3863-efficient-ray-casting-pipeline.md)
This article covers two distinct implementations sharing the name "[Efficient Ray Casting Pipeline](#3863-efficient-ray-casting-pipeline.md)," which differ fundamentally in domain and technique. The first is a software-based 2D raycaster for unstructured grid visualization that minimizes per-pixel cost by rendering to a low-resolution internal framebuffer and upscaling. The second is a [hardware-accelerated Direct Volume Ray Casting](#5442-hardware-based-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) (DVR) pipeline for DirectX 11 that uses [geometry shaders](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md) for active brick detection and ray generation. Both aim to optimize rendering performance by reducing redundant calculations, though they achieve this through resolution scaling versus hardware-specific shader stages respectively.

### [GPU-Driven Architecture](6408-gpu-driven-architecture.md)
An architecture where the [residency octree](#4950-residency-octree.md) and renderer are fully implemented on the GPU, while the CPU handles high-level orchestration.

### VOGUE Architecture
A volume ray-casting accelerator aimed at interactive volume visualization in single-user workstations, characterized by compactness [S2]. It maps an efficient [image order ray-casting](#3161-image-order-ray-casting.md) algorithm directly onto a pipelined architecture [S2]. Higher rendering performance is achieved by distributing subvolumes of the dataset among several basic units interconnected by a high-speed network [S2]. The dataset is partitioned and distributed over multiple units to allow for a high degree of modularity [S2]. It maintains a fully pipelined architecture for shading and classification operations [S2]. It supports up to 64 basic units [S2]. [VOGUE](#1282-ray-marching-traceray-with-shading.md) partitions the dataset among multiple units, whereas VIRIM replicates memory and Cube-3 uses a single skewed memory [S2].

### Hardware-Assisted Ray-Casting
A ray-casting method that does not require sorting volume cells but relies on auxiliary data structures [S3, unofficial]. It reads the volume from texture and cannot benefit from VBOs and continuous streaming [S3, unofficial].

### Pinned Memory Data Transfer
Helper function to transfer triangle mesh data to CUDA-managed unified memory, available since CUDA 7.x [S4, unofficial]. Legacy helper function for CUDA versions < 7.x, using page-locked host memory and explicit device memory allocation [S4, unofficial]. It allocates memory using `cudaMallocManaged`, iterates through mesh faces to extract vertices, and copies data to the device array [S4, unofficial]. For legacy versions, it allocates page-locked host memory, copies vertices to it, allocates device memory, and copies to the device using `cudaMemcpyDefault` [S4, unofficial].

### OpenCL Staging Buffer Commit Flow
CPU writes changes to a staging buffer in system RAM [S5, unofficial]. CPU initiates a parallel copy of the staging buffer data to the GPU [S5, unofficial]. GPU executes the render kernel [S5, unofficial]. It requires two OpenCL command queues and events to ensure commit starts after copy completes, render starts after commit completes, and next copy starts after commit completes [S5, unofficial]. OpenCL was chosen over CUDA (excludes many GPUs), Compute Shaders (insufficient low-level control), and Vulkan (too large/complex) [S5, unofficial].

### OpenCL Acceleration
Attempt to speed up parallel computations using Nvidia Quadro FX 1800 graphics card with OpenCL FFT and custom PyMSES Slicemap implementation [S6, unofficial]. Code has to give the graphics card a lot of work to do to balance the data-to-device transfer overhead; speed increase only on specific cases with long parallel computation [S6, unofficial].

## Background
The approach is supported by NVIDIA, AMD, and mobile graphics cards/processors [S1]. Shader support includes HLSL/GLSL (OpenGL/ES 3.0+, Shader Model 3) [S1].
